prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its development to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, opening new precision tests of fundamental physics

statement.case_for: I keep B025 with Katori and Ye, unchanged from round 1. Round 1 produced no scientific objection to maturity or reproducibility: independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB) agree near 1e-18, and all eight proposers named the same two people. The idea is specific and originated: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice makes the ground and clock states see the same trap depth, which removes the old trade-off between atom number and motional or light-shift systematics. Ye's programme then took accuracy and stability to the limit and brought in many-body effects, spin exchange and collective shifts, which are statistical physics in their own right and not only instrument engineering. For the chair's scope question, I would frame the prize as an invention that has already produced new physics, not as a metrology capability: it is distinct from the 2005 comb prize (a tool for counting optical cycles) and the 2012 ion-control prize (single quantum systems), because the lattice clock is the first scheme to combine very many neutral atoms with negligible trap perturbation, and it is what makes constants-drift and gravitational-redshift tests at the centimetre scale possible. A single-achievement prize with two names is also the most compact and least contested configuration available.
statement.case_against: The discovery-versus-capability objection is real and I do not dismiss it: the largest payoffs (a redefined second, relativistic geodesy, dark-matter and constant-drift searches) are still largely prospective, and the neighbouring 2005 and 2012 prizes mean the citation must be worded tightly. Attribution at the margin remains open for Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Sterr, Gill and Hinkley, and a two-name credit cannot capture them. I also hold the 1e-18 figures and the chronology of the first lattice clocks from recollection, as several colleagues do. Finally, in preferring B025 I am putting maturity ahead of the larger conceptual opening of B022, which I still regard as the most exciting physics on the list.

responses.point: Danielsson, the only member still preferring B022 (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer), frames the choice as a discovery of a new phenomenon against an instrument advance, and asks whether a lattice-clock prize rewards a capability rather than physics.
responses.response: I opened with B022 first and share his view of its scientific appeal, and I agree with him that Bistritzer must not be dropped from any B022 credit, since the 2011 prediction is the origin of the whole field. Where we differ is the criterion. Invention is an explicit category in the will, and the lattice clock is not merely a refinement: the magic-wavelength idea changed what is physically possible and has already yielded new physics in the form of many-body and collective-shift effects and the most stringent redshift and constants tests. I also take his own point from round 1 that the pairing mechanism is open and the experimental credit extends beyond Jarillo-Herrero (Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Young, Kim); I would not call B022 premature, but I do not think the unsettled mechanism is disqualifying for a later cycle, and I do not think it should displace a mature, uncontested case this year. I would not object strongly if the committee preferred B022.

responses.point: Olsson asks the committee to state exactly what is new relative to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, to acknowledge the early strontium contributors, to check her own possible proximity to Katori through Japan, and to verify the 1e-18 figures and chronology against primary intercomparisons before the citation is fixed.
responses.response: I agree on the verification point and think it should be a condition of the citation: the claim should rest on published systematic budgets and cross-laboratory comparisons, not on recalled numbers, and where those do not support 1e-18 the wording should say 'near' or give the level actually demonstrated. On her recusal question I read her documented tie as institutional and general, with no collaboration or co-authorship with Katori or Ye, so I would not require recusal, though I leave that judgement to her and to the chair. I also agree with her that the delivered citation should mention the lattice concept explicitly and not precision spectroscopy in general, so that the neighbouring 2005 and 2012 prizes are not restated. On B008, which she ranked first on her opening ballot, I respect her discounting of her own field, and I would add that its support remains a single ballot.

responses.point: Kroll cites the Charpak and Hall-Haensch precedents for rewarding measurement inventions and flags that Ye also appears on the thorium-229 nuclear-clock candidate, so any B025 decision should be coordinated with it.
responses.response: The precedent argument seems to me right: the committee has repeatedly rewarded inventions that opened new measurement regimes, and the criterion is originality plus demonstrated consequence. On thorium, I would not let a prospective nuclear clock reduce Ye's credit now. The nuclear transition is not yet a clock operating at the lattice-clock level, so it is a possible later development, and a later prize on it would rest on different physics. I disagree slightly with him that the nuclear-clock question is a reason for caution; I would treat it as an argument that Ye's role is a research programme and not a single result, which supports a citation worded around the lattice clock itself.

responses.point: Lindroth, asked by the chair whether Ye's role is better seen as an accuracy and many-body programme or a distinct invention, and who stresses the atomic-structure basis of the magic wavelength and the feedback to fundamental physics.
responses.response: I read Ye's role as the realisation and the extension of the lattice clock to a many-body, record-stability instrument, not a separate invention, which is why I keep the citation to a single invention shared by two names. Her atomic-structure argument also answers part of the discovery-versus-capability objection: the magic wavelength rests on polarizability calculations and the clock now tests physics beyond the standard model of atoms, so the feedback she describes is a physics result and not only an engineering one. I agree with her that the acknowledgment of Lemonde and the SYRTE and PTB groups belongs in the committee's deliberation material even though they cannot be in the name list.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a distinct invention from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes and not as an extension of them.
How Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Sterr, Gill and Hinkley should be weighed against the two-name credit, and whether the citation should acknowledge them.
The exact demonstrated uncertainty levels and the chronology of the first lattice clocks are from recollection and not verified against primary intercomparisons.
For the fallback B022, whether Bistritzer should be named alongside MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, and how the experimental credit beyond Jarillo-Herrero should be handled.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. I have no documented connection to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer, and my listed co-authors and institutions do not overlap with the shortlisted credited names. I have noted the disclosures of Olsson, Kroll and Johansson and see none that I would regard as requiring recusal on B025.
